docs/citable-views.md 5.8 and 10.9 (Edward Lasker, paraphrased from our sheet)
[H] marked guess about nearby pieces: unsourced hypothesis

steps.text: A piece is **defended** when a friendly piece could capture on its square and so take back. A piece nobody defends is **loose**, and taking it wins the piece unless the capture itself walks into something, so check that too. A black pawn captures down the board. The next board is the position you just tried: first the capture, then the answer.

steps.caption: The rook attacks the bishop on g5. The pawn on h6 defends it. The pawn on g6 stands in front of it but cannot capture on g5.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop for 3 points.
The h6 pawn recaptures. The g6 pawn could not have. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The bishop on e6 is loose: no black piece attacks that square. The knight can take it safely.

line.say: The knight takes the bishop and nothing can capture the knight there.
Nothing can retake here. White has won a bishop.

steps.text: A defender must be able to capture on that exact square, **using its own kind of move**. A pawn defends the two squares diagonally ahead of it. A knight defends by its jump, a bishop along its diagonals, a rook along its lines, and a queen both ways. A piece in the way blocks a line. Standing close counts for nothing. A **pinned** piece, one that cannot move without exposing its king, may be unable to recapture: check first.

steps.caption: A pawn defends diagonally forward. For Black, the pawn on d6 covers e5, so the knight is defended.

line.say: The rook takes the knight, winning 3 points.
The pawn takes back diagonally. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The black pawn on e4 is right below the knight, but pawns capture diagonally forward. It attacks d3 and f3, not e5.

line.say: The knight takes. The pawn on e4 cannot capture it, because pawns never capture straight ahead.
Nothing of Black's can take the knight. White has won a knight.

steps.caption: Black to move. A white pawn defends diagonally forward, which for White means up the board. The pawn on e4 covers d5.

line.say: The rook takes the knight, winning 3 points.
The white pawn takes back. Black gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The knight on f6 jumps to d5, so it defends the bishop.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop, winning 3 points.
The knight jumps to d5 and takes back. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The knight on e6 is one step from the bishop, but its jump does not reach d5. Close is not the same as defending.

line.say: The rook takes the bishop. The knight on e6 cannot reach d5.
Black has no recapture. White has won a bishop.

steps.caption: A bishop defends along its diagonals. The bishop on e6 and the knight on d5 touch corner to corner, so the knight is defended.

line.say: The queen takes the knight, winning 3 points.
The bishop takes back along the diagonal. White gave 9 for 3.

steps.caption: The d5 square is light. The black bishop on f8 stays on dark squares, so it can never capture there.

line.say: The queen takes the knight. The bishop on f8 cannot reach a light square.
Black has no way to take back. White has won a knight.

steps.caption: The rook on d8 faces the knight down the file, but its own pawn on d6 stands between them. A blocked line defends nothing.

line.say: The rook takes the knight. Black's rook cannot see past its own pawn.
Black cannot recapture. White has won a knight.

steps.caption: A clear long line does defend. The queen on b8 reaches e5 along the open diagonal, so the knight is defended from far away.

line.say: The rook takes the knight, winning 3 points.
The queen takes back along the diagonal. White gave 5 for 3.

steps.caption: The bishop on e6 touches the knight on d5, but the rook on e1 pins it to the king on e8. A pinned piece cannot capture, so it defends nothing.

line.say: The queen takes the knight. The bishop cannot retake, because moving it would expose its king.
Black cannot recapture. White has won a knight.

steps.text: **Remember.** A piece is defended when a friend could capture on its square and take back. If nobody can, it is loose, and taking it wins the piece. Ask of each friend: can it capture on that exact square with its own kind of move? Pawns defend diagonally forward, a blocked line defends nothing, and a pinned piece may be unable to recapture.
